If it is considered a treaty.

Jimmy Carter unilaterally withdrew the US from a mutual defense treaty with China without Congressional approval. Barry Goldwater sued alleging that he could not do so without the approval of the Senate. The Treaty Clause (Article II, Section 2, Clause 2) gives the president power to negotiate treaties, and the Senate has to confirm them. The idea is that the treaties have the force of law once the Senate approves them. But the U.S. Supreme Court sided with Carter when he withdrew from the mutual defense treaty with China. See Goldwater v. Carter, 444 U.S. 996 (1979). They sent the case back to the District Court with instructions to dismiss the complaint on grounds that it was a political question. So it is within the authority of the president to void a treaty approved by the Senate. George W. Bush also unilaterally withdrew from the ABM Treaty, and the courts refused to intervene. In that case the NATO Treaty says (in full):

Article 13 - After the Treaty has been in force for twenty years, any Party may cease to be a Party one year after its notice of denunciation has been given to the Government of the United States of America, which will inform the Governments of the other Parties of the deposit of each notice of denunciation.

But NAFTA and the TPP may just be considered "statutes" enacted under "trade promotion authority" procedures. Implementation of statute falls almost exclusively on the Pres and his crew, which have very broad practical ability to defang statutory schemes it doesn't like. Congress has shown little willingness to use its constitutional prerogatives to make the Executive Branch do everything that authorized by statute. So, could Pres.
